title: Nine links added in the newer database lists have no index, so removing a member, a staff login or a gym reads those lists for every gym
what: Several lists added in this stretch of changes point at a member, a staff login, a gym or a payment record without an index on that link: plan requests and report requests (member), trainer questions (who it was sent to and who answered), the phone pop-up queues, report files and free-trial numbers (gym), and MettleUp payments (ledger line). When the thing they point at is removed, the database has to read the whole list across all gyms to find the matching lines. The database's own advisor flags all nine. Small today; it grows with every gym.
expected: Every link has an index that starts with the linked column, so a removal touches only its own rows.
how_often: each time a member, staff login or gym is removed
fix_line: Add one index on each of the nine links in a small additive change

title: Opening the leaderboard adds up the whole gym's last 30 days about eight times
what: Each time a member opens the leaderboard, the database adds up every member's last 30 days separately for the top 10, again to find the member's own total, and again to count who is ahead, for workouts and then for kg; it also counts the month's members and the challenge hitters the same way. With 500 members that is about 15,000 day lines read eight times per opening, and the owner's view does it again. Nothing keeps the answer between openings.
expected: The 30-day totals are worked out once per opening (or kept for a minute) and the top 10, the member's place and the counts all come from that one result.
who: members of big gyms and their owners
fix_line: Work out the 30-day totals once per call and rank, find and count from that

title: The nightly backup builds the whole database as one answer, so it will stop working once the data gets big
what: The nightly backup reads every table, every row, into one single answer inside the database and sends it in one go. The database has a hard size limit for one such answer (a few hundred MB), and the whole copy must also fit in memory and in one call's time. Workout cloud copies and check-ins grow every day, so at some point the backup will fail every night, and there is no way to take it in pieces.
expected: The backup reads the database in pieces (per table, or per table in pages) so it keeps working however big the data grows, and a test checks a large copy.
who: every gym, if a restore is ever needed
how_often: every night once the data passes the limit
fix_line: Read the backup in pages per table and stream them into the stored parts

title: The desk's plan request list reads every request the gym ever had
what: The desk's list of pause and renew requests asks for pending ones or ones decided in the last 14 days. The decided time has no index, so the database reads every request the gym ever had each time the list loads, and the index made for this list is never used (the advisor says so). It grows with every request, year after year.
expected: The list uses an index on status and decided time, so it reads only pending and recent requests.
how_often: each time the requests list loads
fix_line: Add an index on gym, status and decided time, or split the read into pending plus recent
